newsitem.title: USA: UN says Iraq at 90-day cap, barring oil price drop.
newsitem.headline: UN says Iraq at 90-day cap, barring oil price drop.

text.p: U.N. overseers approved a 36th Iraqi oil contract late Wednesday, but the sale will fall in the second 90-day period of the six-month oil-for-food accord, all but assuring the completion of first-half deals.

Western diplomats and U.N. officials, while hedging their bets against a drastic decline in world oil prices, said Thursday that the ceiling for $1 billion worth of sales for the first 90 days had been approached, if not met.
"The target of $1 billion for oil sales for the first-three month period has more or less been met," U.N. spokesman Fred Eckhard said.
Western diplomats said the looming March 9 deadline for first period liftings all but prevented further sales.
"It will have to be second period," said a diplomat on any new contracts, noting there was not enough time before Sunday.
But, even that could change if a dramatic price fluctuation took place before the deadline, sources noted.
Officials admitted they were holding back from declaring the first period sales over, since just last week the 34th contract approved was thought to have met the cap.
That 34th sale, a 3.6 million barrel sale to the Indian Oil Corp, pushed sales to the brink of the cap, but a subsequent decline in prices altered the math, sources said.
A U.N. official said as long as no price collapse was recorded before Sunday, all sales would be placed in the second tranche running from March 10-June 9.
Final figures for first period sales would be known early next week, diplomats said.
The United Nations would not confirm the buyer of the 36th oil contract, but sources said the recipient was Petrofina of Belgium PETBt.br.
Terms call for lifting 10,000 barrels per day (bpd) of Iraqi crude over the 90 days in the second-half period.
Iraq is allowed to sell $2 billion worth of oil for six months, in order to buy humanitarian supplies for civilians suffering under sanctions imposed after Baghdad invaded Kuwait in August 1990.
A separate $70 million fee was added on top of the first-half sales cap to pay Turkey for pipeline use.
